messages.author: a08a2def4527ebe2
messages.subject: Two-step estimation of hierarchical models
parts:
Hello everyone!

I have the following model: 

data{
int N;
int M;
int K;
matrix[N,M] z_measurements  ;
matrix[N,K] X   ;
vector[N] Y;
}

parameters{
vector[N] z;
vector[K] beta;
real alpha;
real<lower=0> sigma_y;
real<lower=0> sigma_z;
}


model{
for (i in 1:N)
z_measurements[i,] ~ normal(z[i],sigma_z);

Y ~normal(X*beta+alpha*z,sigma_y);
}

The point is that I identify some individual parameters (z) through one module, and then use these parameters in another module. The object of interest is primarily the beta-vector and the alpha-parameter. In reality my model is more complex, where the individual measurements come from ordinal models. 

So my problem is the following: it takes a long time to estimate this model (several days), and I want to run sensitivity analyses by e.g. changing the variables that enter the X-matrix. However, the z-parameters shouldn't change when I make changes to X. So - have someone tried a two-step version of such a model? I.e. where we use the posterior distributions of z, and take this as data for the second step where I identify beta and alpha? 

I know I can take a frequentist shortcut and use e.g. the ML-estimate of z, but I think the uncertainty of the z-parameters might be important. 

Thanks, 
op

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Two-step estimation of hierarchical models
parts:
I'm surprised this takes several days; is N really huge?
If this is indeed the problem, in this case your model is purely Gaussian so you can integrate out z and write the model of y given z_measurements directly.  Then you've removed the N parameters and everything will go fast.
A

messages.author: a08a2def4527ebe2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Two-step estimation of hierarchical models
parts:
Like I said, my model is more complex than the example above. It was just meant as a minimal example to illustrate the question. 

In the real model, z is a matrix of roughly size 30,000*4. z_measurement are ordinal measurements, with around three outcomes per element of z. Y is also a matrix with ordinal outcomes. So it is like a bunch of IRT-models, where I identify latent traits along five different dimensions, and hence close to 500,000 evaluations of the categorical logit to calculate the likelihood. I use 2000 iterations total, 1000 adaptation, with several chains in parallel. I am using standard priors. Model converges nicely, with average tree-size around 6, and generally no divergent transitions. I'm not saying Stan is slow - it is doing lots of work. 

You are right - I'm ignoring feedback from Y and X to z (akin to the "cut" function in Bugs), but it could speed things up a lot. I also doubt it would have a strong influence on the posterior densities of z, at least it hasn't with my data when I make changes to X. So I was wondering if anyone had tried this in a setting where I could pass general, posterior densitites as "data". 

Best, 
op

messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Two-step estimation of hierarchical models
parts:
Any chance it makes sense to run these different tests with good initial guesses on the parameters? If you're happy with the posteriors from your previous estimate and have reason to believe they aren't really changing, then maybe just initialize your new chains with samples from the posterior of one of your previous estimates?

I dunno -- maybe that'd make the warmup easier for Stan and you could get away with less warmup samples. Not sure if it really applies, or what sorta tests you're trying to do. If your inference took days before, in a good case this would still take days (just less days) so I dunno if that means anything.

Ben

If you're happy with the posteriors from your previous estimate and have reason to believe they aren't really changing, then maybe just initialize your new chains with samples from the posterior of one of your previous estimates?
>
> I dunno -- maybe that'd make the warmup easier for Stan and you could get away with less warmup samples. Not sure if it really applies, or what sorta tests you're trying to do. If your inference took days before, in a good case this would still take days (just less days) so I dunno if that means anything.

This is going to get easier in 2.16 when we can initialize mass matrices.

During warmup, we need to get to the typical set and then we need to
draw a large enough sample to allow us to estimate the posterior (co)variance
(aka inverse mass matrix). The initial values only help us get to the typical
set. In 2.16, we should be able to initialize mass matrices, so if you
can do both, then you'll be set and won't need any warmup at all.

- Bob

and even more if there are multiple points with the same predictors
